brief.situation: You are the cloud engineer for Ridgeline Outfitters, a fictional online store on Google Cloud. At 10:00 a security scan reports that bucket ridgeline-assets is public. Last night a developer granted allUsers Storage Object Viewer on the whole bucket so a fulfillment partner could download one export file. The bucket holds the website's product images, which are meant to be public, and fourteen daily exports of customer data, which are not.
handover: The website loads product images straight from ridgeline-assets/img/. The partner needs today's export by 12:00.
The bucket uses uniform bucket-level access. The security lead wants exposure ended fast, the store owner wants the website working, and the privacy officer wants to know who read the files.
howItWorks: The board shows the bucket, a second bucket if you create one, the website and the partner, with what is placed or running in each. Meters show exposure and broken images.
Each task takes your time: start it, then let it finish, which moves the clock by the minutes it takes. The bucket stays public on the same clock until you change it.
When you close the incident, you write the record and explain your reasoning.

writeup.question: For the record: why the exposure had to end first, how you kept the website working, what you can and cannot say about who read the files, and what stops it happening again.

parts.label: Contain first
parts.criteria: Removes the bucket-wide allUsers grant (IAM, since uniform bucket-level access disables ACLs) as soon as the scope is confirmed, accepting a short image outage.
parts.modelAnswer: allUsers had Storage Object Viewer on the whole bucket, so every export was public. With uniform bucket-level access only IAM decides, so I removed the grant at once; broken images for a few minutes cost less than customer data staying public.

parts.label: Who read it
parts.criteria: States that reads through allUsers are not audit-logged (and Data Access logs were off), so the exposure cannot be ruled out and goes to the privacy officer.
parts.modelAnswer: Public reads generate no audit logs, and Data Access logging was off for Cloud Storage, so nobody can list who read the exports. I treated all 14 as exposed and gave the privacy officer the window from 22:40.

parts.label: Stop it recurring
parts.criteria: Separates public images into their own bucket, enforces public access prevention on the data, shares with the partner by signed URL, and limits retention with a lifecycle rule.
parts.modelAnswer: Images now live in their own public bucket, public access prevention is enforced on the data, the partner gets a signed URL that expires, and a lifecycle rule deletes exports after 7 days.

secured.headline: Good: contained, separated, reported
secured.body: You ended the exposure with IAM first, put the images somewhere meant to be public, guarded the data, shared the one file safely and told privacy the truth about the logs.

scoring.modelReasoning: A bucket-wide allUsers grant makes every export public. The bucket uses uniform bucket-level access, so ACLs cannot be set and only IAM matters: remove the grant at once and accept a short image outage, because customer data being public is worse than broken images. Then give the images their own public bucket, enforce public access prevention (storage.publicAccessPrevention) where the data lives, share the partner's one file with a signed URL, and add a lifecycle rule so exports do not pile up. Public reads are not audit-logged and Data Access logs were off, so nobody can say who read the files: report every export as possibly exposed.
